questions.prompt: How would you design a demonstration that separates the effect of adding mass from the effect of increasing stiffness?
questions.answer: Begin with a common reference system. In one comparison increase mass while keeping effective stiffness fixed, and in another increase effective stiffness while keeping mass fixed. Compare oscillation rates, expecting greater mass to lower frequency and greater stiffness to raise it.
rubric: The answer changes one mechanical property at a time against a common reference.
The answer predicts opposite frequency effects for added mass and increased stiffness.

questions.prompt: Why must you know where a small mass is added before predicting how strongly it affects a particular mode?
questions.answer: The mode has different amounts of motion at different locations. Added mass has a larger effect where that mode moves strongly and little effect at its displacement node. The same added mass can therefore affect different modes differently at one location.
rubric: The answer connects the mass effect to the mode’s local displacement.
The answer explains why the same location can produce different effects across modes.

questions.prompt: At the marked region, mode 4 moves strongly while mode 5 has little displacement and strong local stretching. Why can increasing both mass and stiffness lower mode 4 but raise mode 5?
questions.answer: For mode 4 the added mass matters because the region moves, while the added stiffness has little effect where local stretching is small. For mode 5 the mass has little effect at the displacement node, while extra stiffness matters where stretching is strong. The two modes therefore respond in opposite directions at the same region.
rubric: The answer ties mode 4’s decrease to local motion and the added-mass effect.
The answer ties mode 5’s increase to local stretching and the added-stiffness effect.

questions.prompt: In the illustrated /u/ constriction at the free end, why do both F1 and F2 decrease?
questions.answer: Motion dominates at that location for both illustrated modes. The constriction’s mass-loading effect therefore dominates for each, lowering both mode frequencies and hence both formants in this model.
rubric: The answer identifies motion-dominated behavior for both modes at the constriction.
The answer uses mass loading to explain decreases in both F1 and F2.

questions.prompt: Why can the illustrated /i/ constriction lower F1 while raising F2?
questions.answer: Near the illustrated two-thirds location, mass motion dominates for the first mode while springiness dominates for the second. The same constriction can therefore lower the first frequency through its mass effect and raise the second through its stiffness effect.
rubric: The answer assigns motion and mass loading to the first mode’s decrease.
The answer assigns springiness and stiffness to the second mode’s increase.

questions.prompt: How does the illustrated /a/ constriction reverse the first-two-formant pattern of /i/?
questions.answer: At the illustrated one-third location, springiness dominates for the first mode and mass motion dominates for the second. The constriction raises F1 and lowers F2, reversing the directions predicted for the illustrated /i/ constriction.
rubric: The answer states F1 increases and F2 decreases.
The answer explains the directions through the different local roles of stiffness and mass.

questions.prompt: Why should you not conclude that changing only a string’s free or fixed boundary leaves its fundamental unchanged from the two 100 Hz demonstrations?
questions.answer: The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples were separately tuned to a 100 Hz fundamental. They therefore compare their mode patterns at matched fundamentals, rather than holding length and wave speed fixed while changing only the boundary. Under those unchanged physical conditions, the source notes say the fixed–free fundamental would be half the fixed–fixed one.
rubric: The answer identifies the demonstrations as separately tuned examples.
The answer explains why the shared displayed fundamental does not isolate the effect of changing only the boundary.

questions.prompt: Why can adding the same small mass at one location alter one mode more than another mode of the same extended system?

options.text: The modes move by different amounts at that location, so the added mass participates more strongly in one motion pattern than in the other.
options.feedback: A local mass change matters most where the specified mode moves strongly. At a displacement node it has much less influence, so location must be interpreted within each mode shape.

options.text: The mode with less movement at the added mass changes more, because a nearly stationary location contributes the strongest moving-inertia effect.
options.feedback: Added mass participates more where the specified mode moves strongly.

options.text: The added mass changes the local restoring stiffness first, so the frequency shift is predicted from stretching without considering displacement at that location.
options.feedback: This substitutes a stiffness perturbation for the stated mass perturbation.

options.text: The total added mass determines an equal shift for the two modes, while their different local displacements change their visible amplitudes rather than their mass sensitivity.
options.feedback: Local displacement affects the mass perturbation’s influence on each mode.

questions.answer: A local mass change matters most where the specified mode moves strongly. At a displacement node it has much less influence, so location must be interpreted within each mode shape.
rubric: Relate added-mass sensitivity to local mode displacement.
Explain why one location can affect modes differently.

questions.prompt: A constriction raises both effective mass and stiffness in the lecture’s model. Why can it lower one formant while raising another instead of making the two effects cancel?

options.text: The modes have different local motion and compression patterns, so mass loading can dominate one mode while the stiffness change dominates the other.
options.feedback: Mass and stiffness effects are weighted by the local pattern of each mode. Motion-dominated and compression-dominated regions differ, allowing opposite frequency shifts at the same constriction.

options.text: The opposite mass and stiffness directions imply cancellation of the formant shifts, so the two observed spectral changes should instead be assigned to a source-pitch change.
options.feedback: The local mode patterns make the effects unequal. The supplied explanation predicts different filter-resonance shifts.

options.text: Both formants rise because the constriction’s increased stiffness contributes in proportion to the same amount of compression in each mode.
options.feedback: The modes have different local motion and compression, so their perturbation weighting is not the same.

options.text: Both formants fall because the constriction’s added mass is averaged across the tract, making its location and local deformation irrelevant to the frequency comparison.
options.feedback: The perturbation is local. The mode-specific motion and deformation determine the dominant effects.

questions.answer: Mass and stiffness effects are weighted by the local pattern of each mode. Motion-dominated and compression-dominated regions differ, allowing opposite frequency shifts at the same constriction.
rubric: Identify both mass and stiffness changes.
Explain which local feature makes one effect dominate a specified mode.

questions.prompt: For a specified standing-wave mode, which contrast best identifies where a mass change versus a stiffness change matters most?

options.text: An added mass matters most at a displacement node, while extra stiffness matters most at a location with little stretching or compression.
options.feedback: These sensitivities are reversed. A mass at a node moves little, and stiffness acts through deformation.

options.text: Mass and stiffness changes are both strongest at a displacement antinode, since the largest displacement also marks the strongest compression in the mode.
options.feedback: The comparison distinguishes motion-dominated and deformation-dominated locations.

options.text: An added mass matters most where displacement is large, while extra stiffness matters most where stretching or compression is large.
options.feedback: Mass sensitivity follows moving material. Stiffness sensitivity follows deformation, so a mode’s motion and stretching pattern must be read before assigning the dominant effect.

options.text: Mass sensitivity follows local stretching, while stiffness sensitivity follows local displacement, giving the two properties complementary but exchanged spatial roles.
options.feedback: The roles are exchanged: mass follows motion, while stiffness follows deformation.

questions.answer: Mass sensitivity follows moving material. Stiffness sensitivity follows deformation, so a mode’s motion and stretching pattern must be read before assigning the dominant effect.
rubric: Connect added mass with strong local motion.
Connect stiffness change with strong local deformation.

questions.prompt: In the marked region left of center, mode 4 moves strongly with relatively little local stretching, while mode 5 has small motion and strong stretching. What combined mass-and-stiffness prediction follows?

options.text: Mode 4 rises mainly through the stiffness change, while mode 5 falls mainly through added mass because the low-motion region is the more mass-sensitive one.
options.feedback: This reverses the motion and stretching sensitivities shown in the marked region.

options.text: Both modes fall through the mass increase, treating the equal local addition as an equal moving-inertia contribution despite their different displacements.
options.feedback: The mass participates strongly in mode 4 but little in mode 5 at that location.

options.text: Both modes rise through the stiffness increase, treating the marked region as equally deformed in the two patterns despite their different local slopes.
options.feedback: The marked region is relatively flat for mode 4 and strongly stretched for mode 5.

options.text: Mode 4 is lowered mainly by the added mass, while mode 5 is raised mainly by the increased stiffness at that marked region.
options.feedback: The added mass affects the moving region of mode 4, while the stiffness increase affects the strongly stretched region of mode 5. The same local change therefore has different dominant effects.

questions.answer: The added mass affects the moving region of mode 4, while the stiffness increase affects the strongly stretched region of mode 5. The same local change therefore has different dominant effects.
rubric: Use mode 4’s local motion to predict the dominant downward mass effect.
Use mode 5’s local stretching to predict the dominant upward stiffness effect.

questions.prompt: For the illustrated /u/ free-end loading, motion dominates at the constriction for both of the first two modes. Which prediction and explanation match the model?

options.text: F1 decreases and F2 increases, assigning motion dominance to the first mode but treating the second as stiffness-dominated at the same lip constriction.
options.feedback: The supplied /u/ example states motion dominance for both modes.

options.text: F1 and F2 both increase, interpreting the constriction as a stiffness perturbation without the mass-loading contribution in these motion-dominated regions.
options.feedback: The source identifies the mass-loading effect as dominant for the two modes here.

options.text: F1 increases and F2 decreases, assigning the first mode the stiffness-dominated behavior associated with a different constriction location.
options.feedback: That is not the local pattern of this /u/ illustration, which predicts both decreases.

options.text: F1 and F2 both decrease because the constriction’s mass-loading effect dominates the first two illustrated mode responses.
options.feedback: The local pattern determines the dominant perturbation. Motion-dominated behavior in both modes makes the added effective mass lower both frequencies in this /u/ example.

questions.answer: The local pattern determines the dominant perturbation. Motion-dominated behavior in both modes makes the added effective mass lower both frequencies in this /u/ example.
rubric: Recognize motion dominance for both specified modes.
Predict downward shifts of both F1 and F2.

questions.prompt: The illustrated /i/ constriction is motion-dominated for mode 1 and stiffness-dominated for mode 2. The /a/ constriction reverses those roles. Which formant pair follows?

options.text: /i/ raises F1 and lowers F2, while /a/ lowers F1 and raises F2, interpreting motion dominance as the stronger stiffness effect.
options.feedback: Motion dominance weights mass loading. The stated direction pairs are reversed.

options.text: /i/ lowers F1 and raises F2, while /a/ raises F1 and lowers F2 under the illustrated local perturbation comparisons.
options.feedback: Mass-dominated motion lowers a mode frequency, while stiffness-dominated compression raises it. Reversing which effect dominates the two modes reverses the directions of their first-two-formant shifts.

options.text: /i/ and /a/ both lower F1 and F2, treating the constriction’s added effective mass as dominant for both modes at both locations.
options.feedback: The supplied locations have different mode-specific dominance, including upward stiffness effects.

options.text: /i/ and /a/ both raise F1 and F2, treating constriction-induced stiffness as equally dominant for the first two modes at both locations.
options.feedback: The motion-dominated modes have downward mass effects in the supplied comparisons.

questions.answer: Mass-dominated motion lowers a mode frequency, while stiffness-dominated compression raises it. Reversing which effect dominates the two modes reverses the directions of their first-two-formant shifts.
rubric: Apply mass loading to the motion-dominated mode.
Apply stiffness increase to the deformation-dominated mode and state both vowel patterns.

questions.prompt: In the air-chain model, a pair of neighboring air elements moves closer together and later farther apart. Explain what the masses and springs represent and why the change does not require new air particles to appear.
questions.answer: The masses stand for moving portions of air, while the spring-like connections represent the restoring response to changes in spacing. Bringing neighbors closer compresses the same air, and separating them produces rarefaction. The model changes particle positions and distances, rather than creating a new set of particles for each phase. This physical movement is longitudinal along the tube.
rubric: Identify moving air elements and a restoring effect associated with changed spacing.
Explain compression and rarefaction through changing distances among the same elements.

questions.prompt: A local constriction produces almost no measured frequency change in one mode. A student concludes that neither local mass nor local stiffness changed. Why is that conclusion stronger than the evidence supports?
questions.answer: A small frequency change does not identify the individual mechanical changes. The mode may participate weakly in the altered region, or the downward mass contribution and upward stiffness contribution may partly oppose one another. The observation therefore does not establish that both properties stayed unchanged. Examining the local motion and deformation, or isolating mass and stiffness changes in controlled comparisons, would distinguish these possibilities.
rubric: Explain why a near-zero net shift does not establish unchanged mass and stiffness.
Identify weak local participation or opposing contributions and propose evidence that would distinguish them.

questions.prompt: Design a test of the claim that a given mode is more sensitive to added mass at one location than at another. What should stay the same, what should change, and what should you measure?
questions.answer: Use the same system and excite the same identifiable mode in a reference condition. Add the same small mass at the first location, measure that mode’s frequency change, restore the reference, and repeat at the second location. Hold the underlying stiffness, boundary conditions and measurement procedure fixed. Compare the shifts with how strongly the unperturbed mode moves at each location, expecting the larger downward shift where its motion is larger.
rubric: Keep the system, tested mode and added mass comparable while changing location.
Measure frequency changes against the same reference and relate their sizes to local modal motion.

questions.prompt: Suppose you are given the shape of a vowel that is not one of the three worked examples. Explain the steps needed to predict its first two formant changes without assuming that every constriction behaves like /u/.
questions.answer: Locate the constriction along the glottis-to-lips direction and compare that region with each of the first two mode patterns of the reference system. Determine whether local air motion or local compression and springiness dominates for each mode. A mass-dominated response favors a decrease, while a stiffness-dominated response favors an increase. The worked vowels demonstrate this reasoning method, but their direction pairs cannot simply be assigned to a different constriction without checking its location and modal participation.
rubric: Locate the constriction relative to the glottis and lips.
Assess motion versus deformation separately for the first two modes before predicting their directions.

questions.prompt: You want to compare two string conditions using the heights of their spectral peaks. Why should you keep the pickup location and way of exciting the modes controlled, rather than treating every height change as a changed resonance frequency?
questions.answer: A measured peak’s height depends on how strongly its mode is excited and how much that mode moves at the pickup location. The lecture deliberately selects modal amplitudes so that the five peaks are equal at one marked point. Changing the excitation or pickup can therefore change peak heights without moving the underlying mode frequencies. A controlled comparison should keep those factors fixed and distinguish horizontal frequency shifts from vertical amplitude changes.
rubric: Explain how excitation and local pickup displacement affect peak heights.
Distinguish a change in measured amplitude from a shift in the mode frequency.

questions.prompt: A student expects the three-mass system to have frequencies in the ratio 1:2:3 because it has three modes. Use the lecture’s discrete and continuous examples to explain why that expectation fails.
questions.answer: Three moving masses give three independent modes, but the number of modes does not set their frequency ratios. The illustrated equal-mass chain has ratios near 1, 1.848 and 2.414. Integer harmonics belong to the ideal continuous fixed–fixed string under its boundary and wave assumptions. Transferring that rule to a finite chain confuses two different kinds of system.
rubric: Separate the count of independent modes from their frequency ratios.
Use the noninteger three-mass ratios and identify the different assumptions behind the continuous string’s integer harmonics.

questions.prompt: A system can support several modes, but a one-point displacement recording has fewer clear spectral peaks. Give two source-based reasons why the peak count alone is not a reliable count of all the modes the system can support.
questions.answer: The recording contains the modes that are excited and contribute motion at the chosen pickup, rather than a list of every mode the system could support. An unexcited mode contributes no measured component, and a mode with little or no displacement at that point contributes a weak or absent displacement peak. Changing excitation or pickup can reveal additional components without adding another moving mass or creating another supported mode.
rubric: Separate supported modes from excited and locally measured components.
Identify both excitation and pickup participation as reasons for fewer peaks.

questions.prompt: In the two-mode mixture, one mass sometimes moves less than it does in either pure-mode drawing. Explain how that can happen while the physical mass and spring properties remain unchanged.
questions.answer: The mixed displacement is the sum of the two modal contributions at that instant. When the contributions at a mass point in opposite directions, they partly cancel, giving a smaller net displacement. When they point in the same direction, they reinforce. The changing resultant motion comes from adding the existing mode motions, not from repeatedly changing the mass or coupling stiffness.
rubric: Explain the mixed displacement as an instantaneous sum of modal contributions.
Connect smaller motion to cancellation and larger motion to reinforcement without changing mechanical properties.

questions.prompt: Treat this as a hypothetical experiment: repeated, well-controlled measurements of steady laryngeal vibration fail to show the predicted evenly spaced peaks. What would that mean for the stated prediction, and why could the assigned-frequency membrane animation not override the measurements?
questions.answer: That result would count against the stated prediction under the measured conditions and would call for reconsidering the model, its assumptions or its scope. The membrane animation is constructed with illustrative harmonic frequencies, so its evenly spaced peaks follow from that assignment rather than independent measurement of a natural membrane. A demonstration can make a prediction understandable, but it cannot substitute for the experimental evidence used to test it.
rubric: Interpret the hypothetical result as a challenge to the prediction under the tested conditions.
Distinguish deliberately assigned animation frequencies from independent measured evidence.

questions.prompt: The mode atlas scales different panels to similar maximum visible displacement, and the membrane mixture uses a reduced vertical scale. Why would ranking frequencies by the tallest-looking drawing be a poor interpretation of these displays?
questions.answer: Visible height represents displacement after the chosen drawing scale, not how many cycles occur per second. Normalizing the atlas amplitudes helps compare spatial patterns, while reducing the membrane mixture’s scale keeps the summed motion inside its panel. Neither adjustment sets the mode frequency. Frequency should be read from the labels or compared using cycles over the same time interval, with the stated playback slowing taken into account.
rubric: Separate visible displacement scale from temporal oscillation rate.
Use the stated normalization and mixture scaling to explain why panel height cannot rank frequencies.

questions.prompt: Why is the free endpoint a useful displacement pickup for the illustrated fixed–free string mixture, while the fixed endpoint would be a poor pickup for that same purpose?
questions.answer: The fixed endpoint is a displacement node for each allowed mode, so measuring displacement there misses their motion. The free endpoint is a displacement antinode for the illustrated modes, so each contributes a strong displacement signal there. With equal excitation in the demonstration, the free-end mixture has four equal-height spectral peaks. The measurement position helps explain the observed spectrum without changing which modes the string supports.
rubric: Use node versus antinode behavior to compare the endpoints as displacement pickups.
Connect free-end measurement and equal excitation to the illustrated spectrum.

questions.prompt: Explain how the simplified glottis-to-lips air chain can be compared with a fixed–free system even though its particles move longitudinally and the string picture moves transversely.
questions.answer: The comparison depends on the boundary constraints and patterns of displacement, not on drawing the particles along the same path. The simplified glottal end constrains displacement, while the open lip end allows strong motion. Longitudinal air motion can therefore have fixed–free-like mode patterns with the first two uniform-tube resonances in an odd-multiple relationship. The transverse string is an analogy for those constraints, not a claim that air particles follow the curved string outline.
rubric: Identify the constrained glottal end and motion-permitting lip end in the simplified model.
Separate the common boundary-pattern principle from the different physical directions of motion.

questions.prompt: A measured constriction lowers F1 and raises F2. Why is that result consistent with the illustrated /i/ account without by itself proving that the constriction was exactly two-thirds of the way from the glottis?
questions.answer: The direction pair agrees with a mass-dominated first-mode response and a stiffness-dominated second-mode response in the /i/ example. However, a pair of frequency changes is an outcome, not a direct measurement of constriction position. To support the proposed location and mechanism, compare the actual articulatory shape with the reference and examine how the relevant modes move and deform in that region. The example supplies a supported explanation, rather than a unique location-reading rule from two arrows alone.
rubric: Recognize agreement with the illustrated /i/ direction pair.
Separate consistency with an account from direct evidence for the exact location, and name the needed spatial evidence.
questions.topic: Inferring a mechanism from formant shifts

questions.prompt: The air-column display isolates Mode1@F1, Mode2@F2 and Mode3@F3 in separate rows. Explain how to read those rows without treating them as three separate air streams passing through the vocal tract.
questions.answer: Each row isolates a possible resonance pattern of the same air system so its local movement and compression can be examined. Higher modes contain more alternating spatial regions along the same tube. A physical vibration can combine modal contributions, just as the mechanical mixtures add motions in one system. The separate rows are a way to study the components, rather than three independent streams that occupy different tracts.
rubric: Treat the rows as isolated mode patterns of one air system.
Explain why spatial differences and possible superposition do not imply separate physical air streams.
questions.topic: One air system with several resonances

questions.prompt: The reference row has frequency 0.5 Hz, the 4m row 0.25 Hz, and the 4K row 1 Hz. Explain the order of these rates and why it agrees in both motion directions without doing a formula calculation.
questions.answer: The heavier mass changes its motion more slowly under the unchanged restoring effect, so its cycle lasts longest and its frequency is lowest. The stronger effective stiffness changes the same mass’s motion more rapidly, so its cycle is shortest and its frequency is highest. The reference lies between them. Longitudinal and transverse examples have the same rate ordering because the comparison matches the effective restoring stiffness in the relevant motion direction.
rubric: Explain lower rate for greater mass and higher rate for greater effective stiffness through changes in motion.
Relate the matching directional comparisons to effective stiffness rather than visual direction alone.

questions.prompt: In the economic stabilization illustration, the unemployment and inflation curves have peaks and troughs that are pressed flatter. What shared dynamical idea connects that picture to the course, and what would be missing if you tried to use the picture alone as a quantitative prediction?
questions.answer: The shared idea is that a system can fluctuate over time and that changing how it operates can reduce the size of those fluctuations. Flattening the peaks and troughs depicts stabilization, with the caption linking it to avoiding high unemployment or runaway inflation. The illustration does not provide the actual governing relationships, parameter values or measurements needed to calculate a policy’s outcome. It communicates an aim and a pattern of change rather than a complete quantitative model.
rubric: Identify stabilization as reducing fluctuations over time.
Distinguish the illustration’s conceptual pattern from the missing relationships and data needed for quantitative prediction.

questions.prompt: For the ideal two-equal-mass chain, propose what would happen if you increased only the middle coupling’s stiffness. Which pure mode should be more sensitive, and how does the relative movement of its two masses support your prediction?
questions.answer: In the first mode the two masses move together by equal amounts, so their separation does not change and the middle coupling has little deformation. In the second mode they move oppositely, strongly changing that separation and stretching or compressing the middle coupling. A small stiffness increase there should therefore raise the second mode’s frequency more strongly, while leaving the ideal in-phase pattern much less affected. The prediction uses deformation in the chosen coupling, not merely the displacement of an individual mass.
rubric: Compare relative displacement across the middle coupling in the two pure modes.
Predict greater upward stiffness sensitivity for the oppositely moving mode.
questions.topic: A local-stiffness prediction in a small chain

questions.prompt: What is physically different about the membrane patterns labelled (2,1), (1,2) and (2,2), and why are those pairs not simply another way to name the second, third and fourth harmonic frequencies?
questions.answer: The two entries describe divisions along two different directions of the membrane surface. The (2,1) pattern has two half-wave divisions along one direction and one along the other, while (1,2) exchanges those roles. The (2,2) pattern divides both directions. These pairs describe spatial shape. The demonstration separately assigns its displayed frequencies for illustration, so reading the pair as a harmonic-frequency multiplier would confuse a two-dimensional shape label with a frequency claim.
rubric: Describe how the two indices distinguish spatial divisions in two surface directions.
Separate those shape labels from the deliberately assigned illustrative frequencies.

questions.prompt: The longitudinal and transverse one-mass examples oscillate at the same rate. Which explanation fits the conditions of this comparison?

options.text: Their rates match because the same visible travel distance fixes the cycle time, even if the effective restoring strengths of the two arrangements differ.
options.feedback: Equal travel distance does not establish equal frequency. This comparison matches mass and total restoring stiffness, and its transverse amplitudes are enlarged for visibility.

options.text: Their mass and total restoring stiffness in the displayed direction are matched, so changing the direction of motion does not change the rate in these models.
options.feedback: The model matches mass and total effective restoring stiffness. Its two pre-tensioned transverse segments each supply half the reference restoring coefficient, producing the same 0.5 Hz rate.

options.text: Their rates match because each transverse segment supplies the full longitudinal stiffness, giving two complete restoring effects that compensate for the changed direction.
options.feedback: The transverse segments each contribute half the effective restoring stiffness in this model. Together they match the longitudinal total, rather than doubling it.

options.text: Their rates match because a longitudinal spring and a transverse spring have the same restoring action whenever they are drawn with an equal number of coils.
options.feedback: The relevant quantity is effective restoring stiffness in the direction of motion. Coil count in a drawing does not establish that match.

questions.answer: The model matches mass and total effective restoring stiffness. Its two pre-tensioned transverse segments each supply half the reference restoring coefficient, producing the same 0.5 Hz rate.
rubric: Identify matched mass and effective restoring stiffness.
Keep the conclusion conditional on the stated model comparison.
questions.topic: Why directional examples have matching rates

questions.prompt: Lecture 12’s summary line prints stiffness increasing with frequency decreasing, but its later principle and the controlled comparison point the other way. Which interpretation should guide a prediction at fixed mass?

options.text: Increasing stiffness lowers frequency, because returning more strongly toward equilibrium makes the mass stay near its resting point for a longer part of each cycle.
options.feedback: A stronger restoring effect makes the undamped cycle quicker. Remaining close to equilibrium is an amplitude idea and does not explain a slower rate here.

options.text: Increasing stiffness leaves frequency unchanged, because a stiffness change can alter visible excursion while mass supplies the entire timing of an oscillation.
options.feedback: The controlled comparison changes effective stiffness at fixed mass and changes the rate. Both mass and restoring stiffness matter.

options.text: Increasing stiffness first lowers frequency until the mass reaches equilibrium, after which the frequency rises during the return part of the same cycle.
options.feedback: The mode has a characteristic rate under fixed parameters. Its rate is not assigned opposite stiffness effects on successive parts of the cycle.

options.text: Increasing effective restoring stiffness raises frequency, because the same moving mass is returned toward equilibrium more strongly and completes cycles more quickly.
options.feedback: At fixed mass, greater effective restoring stiffness raises frequency. The controlled 4K comparison oscillates faster, and Lecture 13 explicitly corrects the summary arrow.

questions.answer: At fixed mass, greater effective restoring stiffness raises frequency. The controlled 4K comparison oscillates faster, and Lecture 13 explicitly corrects the summary arrow.
rubric: Apply the controlled stiffness comparison rather than the typographical arrow.
Explain the direction through a stronger restoring effect at fixed mass.

questions.prompt: An experimenter changes an axial spring constant but keeps the transverse tension unchanged, then expects the transverse rate to follow the lecture’s thicker-spring row. What issue must be checked first?

options.text: Whether the block was made to move longitudinally as well, since transverse rate comparisons are meaningful only after motion is allowed in both directions together.
options.feedback: The demonstration can compare transverse systems directly. The issue is what changed the transverse restoring effect, not whether longitudinal motion was also enabled.

options.text: Whether the transverse displacement was drawn with the same maximum height, since equal drawing heights are what make two transverse stiffnesses comparable.
options.feedback: Display height can be enlarged independently of restoring stiffness. Matching a drawing scale does not establish the mechanical change.

options.text: Whether the change actually increased total restoring stiffness in the transverse direction, which in the demonstration depends on pre-tension and geometry.
options.feedback: The symbol K denotes total restoring stiffness in the direction of motion. The transverse model obtains it from pre-tension and geometry, so an axial change alone is not automatically the demonstrated transverse change.

options.text: Whether a different mass was used to accompany the axial change, since an unchanged mass prevents a transverse spring adjustment from affecting its timing.
options.feedback: Mass can remain fixed while effective restoring stiffness changes the rate. The missing check concerns the actual transverse restoring stiffness.

questions.answer: The symbol K denotes total restoring stiffness in the direction of motion. The transverse model obtains it from pre-tension and geometry, so an axial change alone is not automatically the demonstrated transverse change.
rubric: Distinguish axial spring constant from effective transverse restoring stiffness.
Use the demonstration’s pre-tension and geometry assumptions.
questions.topic: Effective stiffness depends on the motion direction

questions.prompt: Why is the oppositely moving mode of the ideal two-mass chain faster than its together-moving mode?

options.text: Opposite motion changes the separation between the masses more strongly, so the middle coupling contributes a stronger restoring effect to that coordinated pattern.
options.feedback: The relative motion of the two masses determines deformation of their connecting coupling. The opposite pattern deforms that coupling more strongly and has the higher characteristic rate.

options.text: Opposite motion divides the original masses between two trajectories, so the moving mass becomes smaller even though the same two blocks remain in the system.
options.feedback: The physical masses remain unchanged between modes. The frequency difference follows from their coordinated pattern and the resulting coupling deformation.

options.text: Together motion removes the end constraints for part of the cycle, allowing the first mode to pause until the fixed endpoints begin to restore it.
options.feedback: The endpoints remain fixed throughout both modes. There is no release-and-pause step in the first mode.

options.text: Together motion stretches the middle coupling most, so it stores a stronger restoring effect and consequently takes longer to complete a cycle.
options.feedback: When equal masses translate together equally, their separation changes little. Opposite motion deforms the middle coupling more strongly.

questions.answer: The relative motion of the two masses determines deformation of their connecting coupling. The opposite pattern deforms that coupling more strongly and has the higher characteristic rate.
rubric: Relate the rate difference to relative motion and middle-coupling deformation.
Keep the masses and fixed endpoints unchanged across modes.
questions.topic: Why the two-mass opposite mode is faster

questions.prompt: The two-mass model’s frequencies have ratio 1:√3. Which interpretation respects the difference between a normal-mode number and a harmonic-frequency multiplier?

options.text: The √3 label gives the combined motion’s frequency, while either pure mode separately follows the ratio 1:2 because there are two masses.
options.feedback: The source assigns √3 to the second pure-mode frequency relative to the first. The combined row contains both components rather than replacing them with one rate.

options.text: The √3 label shows that the second pattern is still developing, and after enough cycles the same unchanged chain should settle to twice the first frequency.
options.feedback: The characteristic ratio belongs to the fixed model. It is not a temporary training or settling stage on the way to an integer ratio.

options.text: The second independent pattern is mode 2, but its frequency is √3 times the first because this finite coupled system does not follow the continuous string’s integer harmonic rule.
options.feedback: Mode 2 names the second independent pattern. The finite equal-mass chain has a noninteger frequency ratio, so the integer-harmonic rule for an ideal continuous fixed–fixed string cannot be transferred by mode number alone.

options.text: The second pattern should be renamed mode √3, because the mode’s label must equal its numerical frequency multiplier whenever its ratio is not an integer.
options.feedback: Mode number labels an independent spatial pattern. It does not have to equal the frequency ratio.

questions.answer: Mode 2 names the second independent pattern. The finite equal-mass chain has a noninteger frequency ratio, so the integer-harmonic rule for an ideal continuous fixed–fixed string cannot be transferred by mode number alone.
rubric: Separate mode index from frequency ratio.
Identify the discrete-chain assumption behind the noninteger ratio.
questions.topic: Mode labels are not harmonic multipliers

questions.prompt: The middle mass stays still in the pure second mode of the three-mass chain but moves in the combined row. What accounts for this?

options.text: Combining the modes frees the middle mass from its original connections, replacing its displacement node with a different physical boundary condition.
options.feedback: The same connected system is used in the mixture. Superposition adds modal displacements without releasing a coupling or changing the endpoints.

options.text: A displacement node in the second mode should pin the middle mass in every possible motion, so its movement means that the combined row uses a different mass.
options.feedback: A node belongs to a particular mode pattern. It is not a permanent restraint on the material point for other modes.

options.text: The combined row creates a fourth normal mode whose main feature is middle-mass motion, adding a new degree of freedom to the original chain.
options.feedback: Three moving masses still support three independent modes in the displayed direction. Their sum does not create an additional independent mode.

options.text: The second mode contributes zero displacement there, while the first and third modes contribute nonzero displacements that can make the middle mass move in their sum.
options.feedback: A location can be a node for one mode without being a node for the others. The mixture adds all three contributions, so its middle mass can move through the first and third components.

questions.answer: A location can be a node for one mode without being a node for the others. The mixture adds all three contributions, so its middle mass can move through the first and third components.

options.text: Three moving masses supply three independent modes in the displayed direction, so those higher-numbered independent patterns are not modes of that row’s system.

options.text: The missing patterns belong to that row but need higher playback speed, so a sufficiently fast movie of the unchanged three-mass chain would reveal six independent modes.

options.text: The row’s end springs count as two additional moving masses, but they are omitted from the frequency analysis because the endpoints are fixed.

questions.answer: The displayed chain has N moving masses and N independent modes in one direction. The empty atlas region records modes that do not exist for the smaller system rather than modes omitted for visual reasons.

options.text: The modal amplitudes were selected to give equal measured contributions at that pickup, so the equality reflects the chosen excitation and measurement location.

options.text: Every fixed–fixed string gives equal peak heights whenever its frequencies are consecutive harmonics, because equal frequency spacing forces equal measured amplitude.

options.text: The equal heights mean that every point on the moving string undergoes the same displacement, even though the separate mode drawings use different wave shapes.

options.text: The peaks became equal when the movie was slowed, since uniform slow playback increases lower-frequency amplitudes until they match the higher ones.
options.feedback: Uniform time slowing changes the displayed rate. The source arranges equal pickup contributions by modal coefficients, not by a frequency-dependent amplitude correction.

questions.answer: The source chooses modal coefficients for five equal displacement contributions at the 17%-length pickup. Equal peak heights are an arranged property of that measurement, not a consequence of harmonic spacing alone.

questions.prompt: The fixed–fixed movie shows 100 Hz and 300 Hz modes at slow visible rates of 0.4 and 1.2 cycles per second. What does the uniform slowing preserve?

options.text: The visible rates become the new physical resonances of the string, so the model should now be interpreted as having a 0.4 Hz fundamental rather than the labelled 100 Hz one.

options.text: The two modes acquire the same cycle time because every displayed mode is divided by the same factor, leaving their difference visible only in spatial shape.

options.text: The 300 Hz component should be interpreted as an amplitude three times larger, since temporal rate information is lost whenever a movie runs below physical speed.
options.feedback: The slowed movie retains relative cycle rates. A frequency ratio does not become an amplitude ratio.

options.text: The higher mode still completes three cycles for each cycle of the lower mode, while the labels continue to identify the physical frequencies represented.
options.feedback: Uniform time slowing multiplies all periods by the same factor and preserves relative cycle counts. Physical frequencies and slow display rates are different labels for the represented process and its viewing speed.

questions.prompt: How can the bottom row of the two-mass demonstration show a complicated changing shape without being a third independent normal mode?

options.text: It displays a third mode that appears only when both original modes are excited, increasing the number of independent patterns through excitation alone.
options.feedback: Changing which existing modes are excited does not add another independent coordinate or supported mode.

options.text: It replaces the two component frequencies with their average, producing one new pure mode whose shape merely appears complicated because it is drawn twice.
options.feedback: The source states that the mixture contains both frequencies. It is not a pure mode at an averaged replacement frequency.

options.text: It adds two existing modal motions, each keeping its own frequency, so the resultant motion can change shape while the system still has two independent modes.
options.feedback: A pure normal mode has a coordinated spatial pattern at one characteristic frequency. The mixed row superposes two such motions and contains both frequencies without creating a third independent mode.

options.text: It alternates between the pure modes by changing spring stiffness on each half-cycle, so its extra complexity comes from a continuously retuned mechanical system.
options.feedback: The combined row is an exact sum of motions in one unchanged system. It does not alternate spring properties to switch modes.

questions.answer: A pure normal mode has a coordinated spatial pattern at one characteristic frequency. The mixed row superposes two such motions and contains both frequencies without creating a third independent mode.
rubric: Separate a modal mixture from an additional independent mode.

questions.prompt: The rectangular membrane animation uses peaks at 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz. What conclusion is warranted about the membrane’s natural frequencies?

options.text: The natural frequencies must be equally spaced because fixing all edges places the same consecutive-harmonic requirement on every vibrating surface as on the illustrated string.
options.feedback: The source explicitly says these are not the rectangle’s natural eigenfrequencies. A membrane’s spatial modes and a string’s harmonic rule cannot be equated from fixed edges alone.

options.text: The harmonic frequencies were assigned for illustration, so that animation alone does not establish equally spaced natural frequencies for a real rectangular membrane.
options.feedback: The supplied speaker notes identify the membrane frequencies as an intentional harmonic assignment. They support a visualization of mode combination and spectra while limiting what can be claimed about natural membrane modes.

options.text: The natural frequencies can be recovered by increasing every displayed frequency by the reduced vertical scale used for the combined surface.
options.feedback: The reduced vertical scale changes the drawing’s amplitude. It is not a conversion from assigned frequencies to natural membrane frequencies.

options.text: The natural frequencies are the five displayed values only at the pickup point, while other points on the same unchanged membrane have different natural mode frequencies.

questions.answer: The supplied speaker notes identify the membrane frequencies as an intentional harmonic assignment. They support a visualization of mode combination and spectra while limiting what can be claimed about natural membrane modes.
rubric: Distinguish illustrative frequency assignment from natural eigenfrequencies.

questions.prompt: Why do the illustrated fixed–free string modes fit one, three, five and seven quarter-waves rather than one, two, three and four quarter-waves?

options.text: Each permitted shape must end at a displacement node on one side and an antinode on the other, which the odd numbers of quarter-waves satisfy.
options.feedback: A fixed end requires zero displacement and a free end is a displacement antinode in these modes. An odd number of quarter-waves joins those different endpoint conditions, giving the illustrated odd-multiple series.

options.text: Each permitted shape must put a displacement node at both ends, and odd numbers of quarter-waves supply two nodes while even numbers supply a free-end antinode.
options.feedback: Two nodes describe the fixed–fixed boundary pattern. Here the free endpoint is a displacement antinode, and the proposed odd/even explanation is reversed.

options.text: The even quarter-wave patterns are possible but removed by measuring at the free end, so the missing frequencies result from pickup placement rather than boundary constraints.
options.feedback: The illustrated allowed shapes satisfy fixed–free conditions. The odd series is not generated by hiding allowed even quarter-wave shapes at the pickup.

options.text: The free endpoint adds an extra half-cycle of waiting to every mode, turning consecutive quarter-wave shapes into odd-numbered frequencies through a temporal delay.
options.feedback: The source explains the series by spatial boundary conditions. No endpoint waiting step or additional timing delay is introduced.

questions.answer: A fixed end requires zero displacement and a free end is a displacement antinode in these modes. An odd number of quarter-waves joins those different endpoint conditions, giving the illustrated odd-multiple series.
rubric: Connect quarter-wave counts to different endpoint constraints.

questions.prompt: At one instant, a point in an oscillating mode is on its resting line. What would establish that it is a displacement node rather than a momentary zero crossing?

options.text: A second point is also on the resting line in that frame, because two simultaneous zeros are sufficient to show that both locations remain still throughout the cycle.
options.feedback: Several moving points can cross equilibrium at the same time. Their behavior over time is needed to distinguish a persistent node from an instantaneous zero.

options.text: The point changes from positive to negative displacement across the next two frames, because a node is identified by repeated crossing of the resting line.
options.feedback: A point that crosses from positive to negative displacement is moving through equilibrium. A displacement node remains at zero instead of passing through it.

options.text: The point is assigned the highest mode number in the display, because a higher mode label makes every resting-line crossing a permanent displacement node.

options.text: Following the same point through the cycle shows that it remains at zero displacement while other points continue to move.

questions.answer: A displacement node has zero displacement throughout the pure-mode oscillation. A moving point also reaches zero when crossing its resting position, so the time course distinguishes the two cases.

options.text: The third mode’s local motion and deformation at the constriction are needed to decide how strongly the mass and stiffness changes affect that mode.

options.text: The sign of F1 is sufficient because every higher mode must copy the lowest mode’s response at a given constriction, regardless of its own spatial pattern.

options.text: The average of the F1 and F2 direction arrows is sufficient because the third formant represents their combined frequency rather than another resonance pattern.
